title: The Email That Became an Accusation
source: Website Film 27 catalogue and published essay synopsis

scenes.text: The message arrives. It is polite, correct, almost painfully careful. Before anyone asks what the writer wants to study, someone wonders: was this written by a machine?
Perhaps a tool helped. Perhaps it did not. The puzzle is why a familiar professional tone becomes evidence against the person using it.
We trained young researchers to begin with respect, mention the work, attach their CV, and avoid making a bad first impression.
Now imagine thousands following that advice. Their opening messages converge. We treat the sameness as a new offense, as if we had not written the rules.
For a stranger, the first email is not an opportunity for literary daring. It is a narrow bridge, with a reputation on the other side.
A grammatical suggestion may improve a sentence. It cannot confirm an experiment, supply expertise, or make a weak scientific question worthwhile.
For decades, journals and institutions have relied on editors, templates, proofreaders, and professional polish. That expectation was not invented by generative software.
Notice who feels comfortable declaring that someone else sounds artificial. Would the same judgment be delivered, quite so readily, to a senior professor?
This does not mean every use of AI is harmless. A tool can invent evidence, conceal dependence, or change the certainty of a scientific claim.
That is precisely why scrutiny belongs with the data, the reasoning, the attribution, and the writer's ability to explain the work.
Ask which result is uncertain. Ask why an experiment matters. Ask what observation might prove the researcher wrong. Those questions are harder to fake.
A first email can begin a conversation. It cannot settle a person's intellectual character. Answer the question, then learn who is asking.
